output:
⚠️ COMMUNITY GUIDANCE (Not Official VA Regulations):
There are several factors that go into determining when your effective date will be for your Disability claims . IMPORTANT NOTES: For the purposes of this article, 'initiate a claim' means either an Intent to file or the submission of the claim itself (whichever is earliest). For those who initiated a claim within a year of separation from Active Duty, this would generally be the day AFTER you separated. The month of your effective date you are NOT paid! So for example if you filed on June 1 - July 1 would be the date compensation begins. You are also paid in arrears, one month behind! So using the same example, you filed on June 1, benefits start on July 1 and the government pays you for the month of July at the end of July. So please do not get confused when VA lists your “payment start date” as July 1, but you are not actually paid for July, till the end of July. In RARE circumstances, the VA may allow extensions to filing deadlines and/or consider your claim initiated sooner than it was received. These circumstances are usually tied to significant natural disasters or major technical difficulties at the VA. Due to technical difficulties - intents to file, claims, and/or appeals received August 8, 2023 through August 14, 2023 are considered to be received August 8, 2023. UNLESS doing so would be less beneficial to the Veteran. When VA combines claims together administratively (that were filed on different days), the later initiated claim(s) will NOT be considered as being received on the same day! Effective date determinations can be VERY complicated! So if you think your rater dropped the ball and missed something, filing a Higher Level Review may be a good option for you.

I've got a few people willing to write buddy statements — how do I make sure they line up?
output:
Good instinct to think about consistency — but "consistent" doesn't mean identical. Three statements that all use the exact same phrasing actually look coordinated/scripted, which can hurt credibility rather than help it. What matters is that they don't contradict each other on the facts.

Here's how I'd approach it:
1. Get each witness to independently describe what THEY personally observed, in their own words — don't show them each other's drafts first.
2. Check afterward for factual conflicts (different dates, contradictory descriptions of the same event) and flag those to resolve — not to make the wording match, but to figure out which detail is actually accurate.
3. Each statement should cover what that specific witness is positioned to know — a coworker won't have the same observations as a spouse, and that's fine.

Send me each witness's raw account (relationship, duration, what they observed) and I'll draft each one separately in that witness's own voice.

output:

output:

If the senior rater is able to make an appropriate grant/denial based upon the existing evidence of record they will do so. These DTA errors will be addressed in a de facto supplemental claim, which is opened (at some point). IMPORTANT NOTES: The DRO CAN find a DTA error, confirm and continue, and issue a difference of opinion on separate issues all within the same decision. This supplemental claim will NOT use any new Intents to File ! If the VA is able to grant then any intent to file associated with the prior claim/appeals CAN be used to assign an Effective date - just that the de facto supplemental will not itself use any unassociated intents hanging around in your file. This de facto supplemental claim DOES allow you to submit new and relevant evidence! This de facto supplemental claim is decided by raters who are NOT DROs. These raters are NOT given the extra authority or power that DROs get! If the de facto supplemental claim decision results in another denial you CAN file a HLR on the decision!

Explain Intent to File (ITF) (38 CFR 3.155) for VA disability claims
output:
⚠️ COMMUNITY GUIDANCE (Not Official VA Regulations):
ITFs are active for 1 year from the date the VA receives it; the VA MUST receive a completed claim/supplemental claim within that year for an ITF to be valid. In most cases, an intent to file will provide the Veteran with the earliest effective date; as the intent to file allows the VA to grant an effective date up to a year before the VA received the claim/appeal. However, in the case of an ITF received within a year of separation from Active Duty, the VA can give an effective date of the day after separation. IMPORTANT NOTES: If an ITF is noted to be for both disability and Pension benefits a separate (non-duplicate) ITF is generated for both benefits. ITFs CANNOT be applied to: Claims for Dependents ; Higher level reviews or Board of Veteran Appeals ; and CUE declarations. Prior to July 30, 2021, ITFs could NOT be applied to Supplemental claims . When appeals/ Claims are Withdrawn any associated ITF CANNOT be used again! If the withdraw is taken back in the appropriate time frame the ITF is still applied to the previously withdrawn appeal/claim. ITFs generated automatically by va.gov when you start a claim online ARE used if you file your claim the same day you start the claim! ITFs received (outside of those automatically made by va.gov) on the same day as a claim/appeal are NOT associated with the claim/appeal filed received that same day! ITFs can be shared by any number of appeals/claims so long as they are received on the same day. ITFs CANNOT be shared by claims that are filed later. Meaning, if the VA administratively combines claims the later received claim will NOT be associated with the prior ITF. The later received claim CAN be associated with its own ITF.
Source: Veterans Benefits Knowledge Base - Effective Dates

Explain Applying for VA disability claims
output:
⚠️ COMMUNITY GUIDANCE (Not Official VA Regulations):
File a claim online or use a 21-526EZ for disability compensation. You will want to claim Unemployability , as well as increases for the service-connected condition(s) that make you unemployable. When you file, be sure to provide evidence (supporting documents like a doctor’s report or medical test results) showing that your disability prevents you from holding down a steady job. In addition, you MUST fill out and submit a VA Form 21-8940 with your claim! IMPORTANT NOTES: You CAN claim conditions which are NOT currently service-connected as the basis of your unemployability, so long as they ARE listed on the 21-526EZ and have not been previously denied. If they have been previously denied, then you will need to Appeal those previous denials. But you CAN file that appeal at the same time as your claim for TDIU is running! An attorney, claim agent, or VSO/POA CANNOT sign the TDIU application! ( M21 I.i.2.A.4.b ) On the VA Form 21-8940 block 16: This would be date you couldn’t work AT ALL anymore. If you were still employed after this time but were on leave (paid or not), PLEASE clarify this in the remarks section! Otherwise it may come off as a contradiction that you ‘ worked ‘ past this date. Block 18 where it says: " LIST ALL YOUR EMPLOYMENT INCLUDING SELF-EMPLOYMENT FOR THE LAST FIVE YEARS YOU WORKED " That does NOT mean the last 5 years from today! That means the last 5 years of working history. So if your last job was in Jan 2020, you MUST state the jobs you worked at from Jan 2015 to Jan 2020! If say, you did not have a job from Jan 2015 to Sep 2015, etc. then state you were unemployed during that period of time! If you don't and just leave that period unanswered, you may delay your claim as the VA may have to reach out to you for an explanation. SPECIAL NOTES: If you know a previous employer is out of business, state so on your application. Since a claim for TDIU is considered a claim for increase, if you have been previously denied for TDIU - you do NOT need to file a Supplemental claim for TDIU. If you served in the National Guard or Reserves ( NOT Individual Ready Reserve (IRR)), be sure to list this employment if appropriate! If one of your former employers was (as a CIVILIAN) the federal government, the VA needs to send VA Form 21-4192 to the following address NOT some random Office of Personnel Management (OPM) address… The VA OFTEN fails to do this. So you may want to mention this address to them… to help them do their jobs. Civilian Personnel Records 1411 Boulder Blvd Valmeyor, IL 62295-2603

Explain Statutory Housebound for VA disability claims
output:
⚠️ COMMUNITY GUIDANCE (Not Official VA Regulations):
SMC S (statutory housebound) is awarded to Veterans who have a SINGLE 100% rating and a separate single 60% rating OR multiple ratings that combine VA Math to at least 60%. IE two 40%, or eight 10%, etc. IMPORTANT NOTES: A single disease process/injury CANNOT be considered as a singular 100% rating - if based on combining their separate evaluations. For example: Having Multiple Sclerosis that had residuals that all combine to 100% - would NOT count as a singular 100%. A grant of TDIU, can count as a singular 100% rating. HOWEVER , if the grant of TDIU is based off of multiple conditions, then TDIU CANNOT be used in place of a single 100% rating! TDIU granted off of a lump conditions (PTSD with TBI rated at 70%) is considered a singular condition. However the same is NOT true if the PTSD and TBI (or other conditions) are separately rated conditions (PTSD rated at 70% and TBI rated at 40%). TDIU granted off a singular condition rated UNDER 60% does NOT count UNLESS an Extra scheduler determination is made. Awards of temporary 100% due to Convalescence leave or Hospitalization for a service-connected condition DO count for purposes of establishing a single 100% rating! After the temp 100% ends, entitlement to SMC S will be discontinued if the Veteran no longer meets the criteria for housebound or statutory housebound.
Source: Veterans Benefits Knowledge Base - Special Monthly Compensation (SMC)

Explain Date Entitlement Arose for VA disability claims
output:
⚠️ COMMUNITY GUIDANCE (Not Official VA Regulations):
Only applicable when evidence clearly establishes that the entitling criteria was NOT met when the claim was initiated. Date entitlement arose is a HARD STOP meaning, the effective date in ALL instances CANNOT be earlier than the the date entitlement arose. Unless , you file a timely Appeal or find a Clear and Unmistakeable Error (CUE) , which successfully overcomes the previous finding of date entitlement arose. IMPORTANT NOTES: The lack of a formal diagnosis is NOT itself always considered clear! If for instance you are denied for no diagnosis for a Mental health or Joint condition but then you get a formal diagnosis, you would be fine - so long as you had symptoms before the formal diagnosis. Since it can be argued you always had those issues, you just did not have a formal diagnosis yet. When you see date entitlement arose it is usually due to the condition having a definitive objective medical diagnosis criteria. These are common in conditions that require X criteria to be met such as Diabetes , Hypertension , or Chronic kidney disease . An example of this would be if the Veteran opens an intent to file and there is medical evidence that the claimed condition did NOT exist until a later time. This could be something like having above normal elevated sugar levels (lab findings) and then filing a claim for Diabetes . Due to there being medical evidence that the Veteran did NOT have diabetes till later. Their effective date would then be the date entitlement arose. AKA date the diagnosis of diabetes was given, be it from the C&P exam or at a later doctor appointment. You will also see date entitlement arose in cases of supplemental claims in which a lower severity of a condition is already established during the life of the appeal.
Source: Veterans Benefits Knowledge Base - Effective Dates

output:

I won't have the witness guess at medical causes or diagnoses — 38 CFR § 3.159 values this as lay evidence precisely because it's observation, not medical opinion. Once you give me the specifics, I'll structure it into a clean statement in the witness's voice.

How do I before filing an increase claim?
output:
⚠️ COMMUNITY GUIDANCE (Not Official VA Regulations):
Please review the Rating Schedule to see if your current level of disability qualifies for an increase. That said, the process of filing for an increase is similar to filing for service-connection. You can file for it on the va.gov website and the VA will order new exam(s) to determine the current severity of your condition(s). IMPORTANT NOTES: Filing for increases DOES open your entire file for review. Meaning, if there are Clear and Unmistakable Errors (CUEs) in your file, the VA is duty bound to correct them. This knife does cut both ways! So it can help as well as hurt you. However, most raters will not look outside of the condition(s) you file an increase for; unless there is something blatantly wrong that stands out. You do NOT need to supply evidence that your condition has worsened with your claim!
Source: Veterans Benefits Knowledge Base - Filing a VA Disability Claim

My spouse and my old squad leader both want to write statements. Should they say the same thing?
output:
Good instinct to think about consistency — but "consistent" doesn't mean identical. Three statements that all use the exact same phrasing actually look coordinated/scripted, which can hurt credibility rather than help it. What matters is that they don't contradict each other on the facts.

Here's how I'd approach it:
1. Get each witness to independently describe what THEY personally observed, in their own words — don't show them each other's drafts first.
2. Check afterward for factual conflicts (different dates, contradictory descriptions of the same event) and flag those to resolve — not to make the wording match, but to figure out which detail is actually accurate.
3. Each statement should cover what that specific witness is positioned to know — a coworker won't have the same observations as a spouse, and that's fine.

Send me each witness's raw account (relationship, duration, what they observed) and I'll draft each one separately in that witness's own voice.

output:
⚠️ COMMUNITY GUIDANCE (Not Official VA Regulations):
An opportunity to submit NEW AND RELEVANT evidence. New: The VA did not previously have/consider it. Relevant: Directly addresses the rationale for the denial. For example: If you were denied for having no diagnosis, you need to supply evidence of a diagnosis. New and relevant evidence can take the form of: Being seen by your doctor for the claimed issue(s); New theory of service-connection (claiming your condition was caused by another service-connected disability); This does include Presumptive conditions be they old or recently passed presumptives; Exam willingness - if you were previously denied because you missed an exam, simply state that you are willing and able to attend new examinations; Independent medical opinion (IMO)/Nexus letter ; DBQ ; Personal statements ; or Buddy statements . IMPORTANT NOTES: Remember you have 1 year from the rating decision’s notification letter to file an appeal (if you want to potentially keep your back pay). Which means 1 year to develop additional evidence for your claim. We recommend waiting until you have enough evidence to be successful before filing - your VSO or lawyer can advise you on this. Do not file appeals with insufficient evidence, this just gums up the system for you and other Veterans. Do know you CAN extend this window for by filing an Intent to File (ITF) ! The ITF will give you a year (from the ITF) to gather evidence. While allowing you to keep back pay. If the VA grants an increased rating based upon a supplemental claim, the Effective date does NOT automatically go back to the original claim! If MEDICAL evidence shows an increase is warranted that is dated BEFORE/AFTER you initiated your supplemental claim the effective date will typically be the date of the medical evidence showing an increase was warranted; this typically is the date of your Examination ! Because of this, DO NOT file a supplemental if you disagree with the evaluation, UNLESS you provided medical evidence showing a higher evaluation was warranted this evidence is dated BEFORE the decision which assigned the current evaluation! If you do not have this evidence but feel you should have been rated higher consider filing an HLR or simply an increase claim. Do NOT file a supplemental claim for an evaluation after a year! Even if you have new evidence showing a higher evaluation was previously warranted! If you do, at best the effective date will be the date the supplemental was initiated or at WORST the date of the examination conducted AFTER your filed the supplemental! So in these cases, just file a increase claim! NOTES: Veterans CAN file a supplemental claim ANYTIME after their denial. However, to potentially get back pay from the start, they must file within a year of the last decision. Veterans CAN submit a supplemental claim over and over again. So long as , there is new and relevant evidence being submitted every time . If you need the VA to get non-federal medical records or Vet Center records for you, then you will need to also submit a VA Form 21-4142/21-4142a .
Source: Veterans Benefits Knowledge Base - Filing an Appeal

output:
Good instinct to think about consistency — but "consistent" doesn't mean identical. Three statements that all use the exact same phrasing actually look coordinated/scripted, which can hurt credibility rather than help it. What matters is that they don't contradict each other on the facts.

Here's how I'd approach it:
1. Get each witness to independently describe what THEY personally observed, in their own words — don't show them each other's drafts first.
2. Check afterward for factual conflicts (different dates, contradictory descriptions of the same event) and flag those to resolve — not to make the wording match, but to figure out which detail is actually accurate.
3. Each statement should cover what that specific witness is positioned to know — a coworker won't have the same observations as a spouse, and that's fine.

Send me each witness's raw account (relationship, duration, what they observed) and I'll draft each one separately in that witness's own voice.

Depending on your MOS and/or Combat experiences, your claim of hearing loss may be given additional weight for consideration for service-connection. Which is not to say, if your MOS is not considered at high risk for noise exposure or that you did not see combat that you cannot get service connection. In order to get a proper rating the audiologist conducting the Examination will conduct two tests to determine your hearing loss. Speech discrimination - your ability to understand spoken words. Your examiner will say a word and you repeat it. Your responses are then calculated as a percentage (higher percent, meaning better hearing). Puretone audiometry test - your ability to hear tones. You will sit in a box and press a button when you hear a tone. The tones the VA cares about are 4000, 3000, 2000, and 1000Hz. The results from those tones (how loud the tone had to be before you heard it) are then added together and divided by 4 to give you your average. The lower the number is, the better your hearing is. PRESUMPTIVE CONDITION: Hearing loss is considered a Presumptive condition if it manifests within one year of separation, AND the severity warranted at least a 10% evaluation within that time. NOTE: If you have disabilities that make it impossible/difficult to complete the speech discrimination test you will be rated based on just the puretone test results.
Source: Veterans Benefits Knowledge Base - Rating Schedule for the Ear
